content.title: The Innovation Ecosystem for Sustainable Energy
content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations

content.text:
Lesson 2 explores how to build inclusive, future-ready innovation ecosystems that support sustainable energy transitions in developing countries. It examines strategies to foster clean energy entrepreneurship 💬️, strengthen local R&D capabilities, and promote collaboration between startups, investors, academia, and policymakers.

The lesson highlights the role of academic institutions in technology validation and adaptive innovation, and emphasizes how international actors can evolve from technology donors to co-creators of innovation ecosystems.

Through examples from Kenya, India, South Africa, Vietnam, and beyond, the lesson illustrates how tailored policy, finance, and knowledge-sharing mechanisms can unlock the potential of local innovators.

It also unpacks emerging research areas, solar, wind, storage, carbon capture, and green hydrogen, and stresses the importance of local manufacturing, open knowledge frameworks, and skills development to ensure that energy innovation is both impactful and equitable.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: A: Strengthening local innovation ecosystems in developing countries

content.text:
As developing countries prepare for a just and inclusive energy future, strengthening local innovation ecosystems will be critical to scale clean energy solutions that meet local needs.

Clean energy transitions are expected to generate 14 million clean energy manufacturing jobs by 2030, more than doubling from 6 million today, with over half concentrated in electric vehicles, solar PV, wind, and heat pumps (IEA, 2024).

However, this opportunity is not automatic: up to 80% of cleantech ventures in developing countries fail within their first five years mostly because of weak ecosystem support.

To address this, innovation strategies must move beyond high-tech R&D and focus on evaluating, adapting, and deploying unfamiliar technologies that suit local geographic and social realities. In Kenya, for example, the off-grid solar PV sector thrived through policies that rewarded local service innovation, building on the country’s strength in digital finance.

Other countries are leveraging existing industrial capacities: Mexico in solar PV manufacturing, Brazil in bioethanol innovation, and Kazakhstan in adapting oil and gas expertise for clean fuels.
Despite this potential, five major ecosystem gaps persist:

content.title: Limited access to testing and validation facilities

content.text:
To fill these gaps, enabling functions, such as product prototyping, pilot testing, incubation, IP support, and business model validation, must be systematically embedded. Governments and ecosystem conveners are encouraged to take on “ecosystem connector roles,” facilitating structured collaboration across actors.
Establishing Cleantech Innovation Clusters can further serve as focal points for technology development, policy feedback, and market engagement.

Academic and research institutions are foundational to future-ready energy innovation ecosystems. Their role extends far beyond education: they are instrumental in validating cleantech solutions, supporting early-stage technology development, and advancing technology readiness assessments. As part of the broader “resource push” pillar, their contributions include conducting proof-of-concept testing, piloting, and providing technical advisory services.


However, many developing countries lack cutting-edge research facilities. To overcome this, new national agencies and technical networks can coordinate existing expertise and link it with national energy and climate priorities. Academia’s involvement in joint labs, standards development, and mentoring entrepreneurs is also critical to ensure innovations are both technically sound and commercially viable.
Several countries already possess underutilized technical expertise:

content.title: India
content.body: has technical capacity in both energy efficiency and biotechnology, but these sectors remain under-leveraged. The country could scale energy efficiency through stronger public procurement standards and expand biotech applications to clean energy through strategic policy support.

content.title: Argentina
content.body: possesses nuclear expertise, especially in small modular reactors (SMRs), but its innovation system remains fragmented. Strengthening coordination and targeted investment could allow Argentina to capitalize more fully on its nuclear R&D potential.

content.title: South Africa
content.body: has historic leadership in synthetic fuels technology but has not prioritized it in clean energy innovation strategies. Revitalizing this area could unlock new low-carbon fuel pathways for the country .

content.text: For these assets to translate into system-wide transformation, academic institutions must actively participate in ecosystem governance platforms such as innovation councils and cleantech roundtables. Mexico provides a strong example, where the INECC is legally mandated to evaluate national climate policy and promote learning, reinforcing the role of research in adaptive innovation.

Looking forward, international institutions must evolve from agents of “technology transfer 💬️” to enablers of “innovation co-operation.” This shift reflects the growing value of mutual learning and co-creation between countries. Many developing nations have pioneered globally relevant solutions, such as mobile finance and battery swapping.
International actors play a vital role in aligning siloed stakeholders, such as governments, startups, and academia. They can offer guiding frameworks for actor engagement, tailored to local contexts. For instance, the proposed global framework for cleantech ecosystems can be localized with support from international partners. Equally important is investment in ecosystem diagnostics, baseline mapping tools that identify gaps in technical infrastructure, institutional roles, or policy linkages.

UNIDO and others recommend supporting multi-country peer learning platforms, establishing regional hubs of excellence, and facilitating cross-border exchanges focused on coordination and innovation policy design (UNIDO, 2024). Since 1992, 74 Technology Needs Assessments (TNAs) have been completed under UN climate mechanisms, but many underrepresent local innovation potential (IEA, 2024). International fora like Mission Innovation and the UNFCCC Technology Mechanism can help reposition national strategies within global knowledge networks.

Ultimately, future-focused international collaboration should help EMDEs build innovation ecosystems across four critical pillars: resource push, knowledge management, market pull, and socio-political support, ensuring sustainable energy innovation is locally grounded, globally informed, and equitably distributed.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: B: Collaboration between startups, investors, and policymakers

content.text: Pathway for scaling up innovations and pilot projects

Scaling up clean energy innovations in developing countries requires strategic collaboration between startups, investors, and policymakers.

One relevant approach is aggregating Distributed Renewable Energy (DRE) projects, such as solar mini-grids, into bankable portfolios. Bundling small-scale initiatives not only enhances economies of scale and reduces costs but also improves energy resilience through coordinated deployment and management.

For instance, Kenya’s Lake Turkana Wind Farm mobilized USD $870 million to develop a 310 MW facility, leveraging a 20-year Power Purchase Agreement, public-private partnerships 💬️, and guarantees from the Kenyan Government, the African Development Bank, and the Danish Development Fund (WEF, 2019).

Similarly, South Africa’s Renewable Energy Independent Power Producer Procurement Programme (REIPPPP) attracted USD $135.6 billion in investment, with 25.8% coming from foreign investors, than ks to streamlined public-private coordination and clear tendering frameworks.

However, despite these successes, significant challenges persist. Less than 2% of global climate tech venture capital currently goes to Africa. To change this trajectory, targeted interventions are needed to de-risk early-stage ventures and create enabling environments with clear policies, stable market demand, and technical support.

Startup incubators and accelerators serve as vital engines for energy innovation, particularly in emerging markets where startups face fragmented funding ecosystems, inadequate infrastructure, and limited global exposure.

The undp accelerator labs 💬️, operating across 91 labs in 115 countries, play a central role in nurturing bottom-up energy solutions by connecting grassroots innovators, researchers, and private sector actors (UNDP, 2023). These labs accelerate the adaptation of frontier technologies to local contexts, facilitate real-time learning on what works, and foster continuous feedback loops with policymakers to strengthen impact.

National innovation accelerators are equally important in improving the market readiness of climate technologies by offering structured support for prototyping, testing, mentorship, and investor matchmaking. To this end, several countries have established green innovation hubs, often with blended funding from public and philanthropic sources, aimed at supporting startups working on energy access, energy efficiency, and clean cooking.

These efforts are essential to align innovation with local energy needs and broader climate resilience goals, ensuring that the energy transition is both inclusive and future-ready.
